We thank the reviewers for their interest in this specific analysis. 
To examine the influence of key factors on attack success rates (ASR), we construct, for each experimental configuration (defined by target model, surrogate pool, scenario type (HoS, HeS, or HoS) and $\varepsilon$), a feature vector comprising:

- A one-hot vector from the target which has a $1$ in the 1st,2nd,3rd entry if the model is a resnet, pure_cnn, transformer-like model respectively;
- A one(s)-hot vector from the pool of surrogates following the same principle, i.e., the vector has $1$ in the 1st,2nd,3rd entry if the pool of surrogates includes a resnet, pure_cnn, transformer-like model, respectively;
- A one-hot vector from the typology of scenario deduced from the categorical variable “Scenario Type”.
- The value of eps has been included

We would like to clarify a possible ambiguity: it is unclear whether the reviewer is suggesting a full factorial experimental design, such as selecting surrogate pools via a statistical Design of Experiments framework, i.e, asking for a complete factorial analysis to infer the composition of the pool of surrogates based on the available models. If that is the case, we want to highlight that such a selection of the surrogates is computationally infeasible due to the combinatorial explosion of experiments that would be in the order of $\binom{N}{K+1}$, where $N$ is the amount of models to use as target and surrogates, and $K$ the maximum dimensionality of the surrogate pools. Furthermore, such a selection should be made involving one or more fixed attacks, which would inevitably produce a biased choice of the pools.

To fulfill the purpose of this benchmark—one of which is to unveil bad practice during the evaluations of transfer-based attacks currently adopted in the literature— it has been enough to select a fixed subset of targets and a fixed subset of surrogates. The composition of the surrogate pools is based on consideration of the architecture of the models, which has been discussed in the paper, and which therefore is highly supported by the a-posteriori analysis summarized below and sketched in the previous answer. This setup avoids cherry-picking and enables a controlled study of the factors influencing ASR.

Below, we analyze the impact of the factors via a correlation analysis deduced by fitting a linear model to predict the ASR from the features described above. Results are interesting and reported in a table below, which will also be included in a dedicated section in the supplementary material.

**Table** - Linear model coefficients predicting ASR from configuration features.

|res_target|cnn_target|vt_target|res_surr|cnn_surr|vt_surr|etero|omeo|robust|eps|
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
0.16|0.13|-0.09|0.02|0.01|0.035|0.05|0.25|-0.28|0|



**Discussion of the Results**: 
The analysis shows that transformer-based targets correlate negatively with ASR, while CNN and ResNet targets have a positive correlation. The architecture of individual surrogate models contributes little when considered in **isolation**, but their **joint** configuration significantly affects ASR. Notably, robust surrogate pools are associated with lower ASRs, and homogeneous scenarios yield higher transferability—confirming observations from bar plots and tabular data elsewhere in the paper.

**Key Message**: 
This analysis confirms that while target architecture impacts attack transferability, the strongest influence comes from the **relationship between target and surrogate architectures**, rather than the presence of a specific model type in the pool.

We thank the reviewer for the thorough analysis and valuable comments. We will revise the manuscript accordingly to address the raised concerns. In detail

**Section 6 - Ethical Considerations and Broader Impacts**:

A new section will be included in the main paper, before the conclusions, to address the following aspect:

*Acknowledge the Dual-Use Nature*: We will summarize what intent can be considered harmful and what is instead harmless, explicitly suggesting beneficial usage of the tool to enhance robust and safe AI models, and facilitating proactive red-teaming strategies.

*Detail the Positive Societal Impacts*: We will make clear that TransferBench offers a standardized framework to evaluate defenses, improves understanding of real-world attack limitations, and supports proactive red teaming to identify and mitigate vulnerabilities before deploying models.

*Detail the Negative Societal Impacts*: We will highlight that there is a potential risk that TransferBench, due to its efficiency and ease of use, could lower the barrier for malicious actors. Moreover, the goal of advancing more reliable and query-efficient black-box attacks might be perceived as enabling the development of stronger offensive tools. Nevertheless, we will highlight that Positive impacts outnumber negative ones, fostering the research of dedicated defences against transfer-based attacks.

 **Update Checklist**: We will update Questions 10 and 11 in the checklist to “[Yes]” and reference the new Section 6 as justification.

Below, we present a draft of the new section **Section 6 - Ethical Considerations and Broader Impacts** that will be added to the final version of the paper. 

```
\paragraph{Responsible Use of the Benchmark.}
While tools for generating and evaluating adversarial examples can advance our understanding of model vulnerabilities, they also present inherent dual-use risks. To address this, we clearly define the intended use of our tool as a resource for defenders, i.e., researchers and practitioners focused on strengthening model robustness and advancing adversarial defense strategies. 
Acceptable uses are strictly limited to research aimed at improving model robustness, advancing secure AI system design, and enhancing the evaluation of adversarial defenses, facilitating proactive red-teaming strategies. We explicitly prohibit any offensive applications, including but not limited to unauthorized security testing of live systems, surveillance, privacy violations, or the deployment of adversarial attacks for malicious purposes. As highlighted in our recommended practices, the evaluation of adversarial attack performance is intended solely to inform and improve safety measures, not to exploit model vulnerabilities.

\paragraph{Safeguards and Mitigation Strategies.} To reduce the risk of transfer-based adversarial attacks that exploit query access to target models, we recommend several mitigation strategies. First, model providers should implement strict access controls, such as rate limiting, authentication, and anomaly detection, to monitor and restrict potentially abusive querying behavior. Defensive techniques like input filtering, adversarial training, or certified defenses can also reduce the effectiveness of surrogate-based attacks. 

\paragraph{Additional Insights from the Benchmark.} Although the primary aim of our benchmark is to support the evaluation and development of defenses, it also reveals important findings. Notably, our results expose a significant gap between the claimed robustness of some defenses and practical resilience in more advanced transfer-based settings. This highlights the need for more comprehensive and rigorous benchmarks that reflect the complexities of available adversarial tools, and encourages the development of defenses that generalize beyond narrow evaluation protocols.
```

rebuttal.value:
We thank the reviewer for the observations. We reply to each of them below. Actions refer to changes to the paper or code, and will only be made public after the final communication as indicated by the NeurIPS guidelines.


**Contribution of our work**. We invite the reviewer to check Table 4 in the appendix provided with the original submission. This table provides an overview of the papers that utilized non-homogeneous pools (HeS)  and robust targets (HoS+R), showing that these choices are (unfortunately) not commonly included in evaluation protocols. This reveals that the heterogeneous scenario is _not_ a widely accepted evaluation setting. Our goal in proposing a benchmark is to reduce this gap in future evaluations and avoid propagating this bad practice. Our contribution lies not only in integrating these under a unified framework, but in systematically highlighting underexplored yet critical scenarios. This goes beyond engineering. It is a first step toward more rigorous and reproducible black-box robustness evaluation. If the reviewer is aware of prior work that already presents similar findings or systematically explores these evaluation issues, we would be happy to include it and cite it in our discussion of the related work.


**Extensible scenarios.** We appreciate the reviewer’s suggestion regarding the need to evaluate more complex and dynamic environments. Nevertheless, TB evaluation has been designed to be extensible in this direction, as it is independent of the choices of the surrogates (grouped into pools that are explicitly defined in configuration files) and the internal logic of attacks. For this reason, also adapting TB to further defences will not require modifying the framework itself.
To further illustrate the extensibility, we implemented a new defended model [1], which includes an active defence based on a detection-rejection mechanism, which does not require any changes in the framework interfaces. The only steps we needed to follow are: (i) importing the backbone-robust model’s weight from the original repo, similar to how previously done for other models; (ii) wrapping the model to return one class more for the rejection mechanism.

We thank the reviewer for the comments and suggestions. Detailed answers are given below. Suggested actions on the paper/code will be publicly available after the final communication.

**Interaction Analysis**
As discussed in Section 4, our benchmark already analyzes three key independent factors affecting attack performance: (i) the choice of surrogate models (Section 4.1), (ii) the robustness of the target model (Section 4.2), and (iii) the impact of query refinement mechanisms (Section 4.3). Each of these factors was studied in isolation to ensure a clear understanding of their individual contributions.
To complement our interaction investigation, we conducted a correlation analysis between attack success rates and both the architecture family of the surrogate models and the type of target model. The analysis shows that CNN and residual targets are generally more vulnerable (i.e., positively correlated with higher attack success rates). At the same time, ViT and robust victim models exhibit strong negative correlations, confirming (as also observed by the reviewer) that state-of-the-art attack methods perform poorly against robust victim models. 
The additional analysis further reinforces our finding that surrogate-target mismatch plays a key role and may overshadow the benefits of other attack refinements. For example, transferability is significantly reduced when attacking a ViT model using CNN-based surrogates, even in the presence of query refinement mechanisms. If the reviewer has some other specific analysis to suggest, we are happy to consider further discussion.


_Action_: We will include the results of the correlation analysis in the revised manuscript and we will expand the discussion to highlight how interaction effects between surrogate and target model families influence transferability.


**Relevance of the experimental context.** 
We thank the reviewer for raising this important point. We would like to emphasize that TransferBench was explicitly designed to address the evaluation biases commonly found in prior work. As shown in Table 4 of the appendix, many previous studies relied on overly favorable setups, such as using homogeneous surrogate sets or omitting robust target models, which can significantly inflate attack performance due to architectural overlap between surrogates and targets.
To address this, TransferBench systematically evaluates attacks along multiple dimensions. It includes surrogate pools that are deliberately non-overlapping with the target models and span different architectural families, such as CNNs, residual networks, and vision transformers. It also incorporates a range of target models, including robust ones, and runs all evaluations on both CIFAR-10 and ImageNet. These design choices were made to minimize the influence of any single architecture, dataset, or evaluation setting, ensuring that the results reflect general trends rather than isolated outcomes.
With respect to SASD_WS, we agree that its strong performance across HeS scenarios is noteworthy. However, we emphasize that this result is not limited to a single configuration. SASD_WS performs consistently well across a wide range of settings (17 in total), including different datasets and target model types. We thus conclude that its effectiveness is not simply the result of a particular benchmark choice, but more likely due to a specific underlying methodology that favors transferability for this attack. We believe this finding highlights the potential of query-free approaches and opens up new directions for future work.
We noticed, SASD_WS is the only method including a DI strategy [1] in the attack pipeline, rescaling and cropping input within the perturbation budget. Unfortunately, we do not have dedicated experiments to support the contribution of this component, but we believe this aspect can be easily covered in future versions of the benchmark, enriching it with a DIM+NaiveAvg baseline for a thorough evaluation.  


_Action_ : We will clarify these points better and discuss the broader relevance of the observed results in the revised manuscript.


**Additional feedback.** We will update the manuscript to clarify that the HeS+R scenario is excluded because it represents an overly pessimistic setting. In our experiments, even attacks using homogeneous surrogate models struggle to succeed against robust targets, which means that non-homogeneous ones will definitely fail. Furthermore, we will also revise the text to clarify that variable z in Equation (3) represents the logits output of the target model g.

We thank the reviewer for the suggestion to improve the evaluation by considering a broader range of perturbation budgets. We agree that this is a valuable direction for future iterations of the benchmark, particularly to increase the difficulty of the Homogeneous Scenario and to better evaluate the vulnerability of robust models.

_Action_: To this end, we introduced two additional scenarios into the benchmark:

- HoS with a smaller perturbation budget of $8/255$
- HoS+R with a larger perturbation budget of $32/255$


The results confirm the main findings of the paper. In the Homogeneous Scenario, as expected, success rates decrease under the tighter budget, but the relative ranking remains consistent. Specifically, the query-free baseline SASD_WS continues to achieve the highest success rate ($42.0%$), while DSWEA, BASES, NaiveAvg100, and NaiveAvg10 yield comparable ASRs of $37%$, $32%$, $31%$, and $30%$, respectively.

In the Robust Scenario, increasing the perturbation budget to $32/255$ does not improve attack success against the Amini-Sw-L [2] and MIM-Sw-L [36] models, indicating that these models remain robust under stronger attacks. 

Such analysis leads to further considerations. Indeed, the Pub-RN-50 [30] model is successfully attacked across all methods, showing even higher success rates with the increased budget. We would like to emphasise that this model has been claimed to be robust specifically against transfer attacks, and our evaluation reveals intriguing weaknesses that invalidate this claim. First, in the original evaluation, the paper did not present an analysis at different perturbation budgets, which is, as the reviewer suggested, very insightful not only to evaluate attacks but also the models’ robustness. Second, we found that the model (i) is weaker than some non-robust models and (2) shows a high ASR even against targeted attacks, which are more difficult to achieve than the untargeted ones adopted in the original evaluation. While this is not a major result in our paper, it is definitely noteworthy to highlight as an additional result attainable with our benchmark.

We thank the reviewer for all the feedback. Replies are organized below.

**Ensemble-based black-box transfer attacks vs ensemble-based attack optimization.** 
The reviewer suggests that the paper could be made “more concise and clear,” particularly by improving the naming of the problem in Eq. 1 and Problem (EBA). While we acknowledge that alternative names are possible, we stress that the distinction between (EBA) and (QBR) was introduced to disambiguate the two phases commonly involved in solving Problem in Eq. 1. Indeed, such a formulation is one of the contributions of this work, wrapping all the ensemble-based attacks in a unique formulation that, as far as we know, has not been explicitly stated in prior works. Specifically, Eq. 1 models the full attack, encompassing both surrogate exploitation and query refinement. In contrast, Problem (EBA) refers to the gradient-based optimization phase applied solely on surrogates, where full gradient access is available. This modeling offers the most precise formulation we found so far, and we believe that further simplification would reduce clarity and soundness. Nevertheless, we can suggest other names to reduce confusion.


_Actions_: To improve clarity by preserving the proposed formulation, we will revise the name of Problem (EBA), e.g., to surrogate-based optimization or local surrogate optimization, to better reflect its role in exploiting surrogate gradients.


**Robust Target.** The robust target imports pre-trained robust models (as it is not the main goal of the benchmark to evaluate defenses). Nevertheless, our benchmark can also produce an evaluation of defenses, as it provides the implementation of a wide choice of attacks. Integrating a defense is indeed possible, and we propose as an example the integration of CCAT [1], a defended model leveraging a detection-rejection mechanism (refer also to the response to reviewer RWWY below). Therefore, TransferBench is highly extensible, allowing the user to create their own scenario (thereby addressing a customizable model), providing a unified, configurable framework that abstracts away low-level details and enforces consistency in evaluation, logging, and model-query interaction protocols.


**Dataset size.** In our benchmark, we consider the Neurips2017-target-benchmark for mainly two reasons: consistency and efficiency. Indeed, the dataset (widely accepted in the black-box attack community, see works in Table 4, Appendix) provides a consistent, standardized choice of the target label, allowing for easy reproducibility and comparison of the results among other papers and benchmarks. 
Furthermore, we would like to remark that in our case, the model is fixed (pretrained), and we are not interested in the variance of the predictor itself. Instead, we only aim to assess the stability of the evaluation metrics (e.g., accuracy, ASR, number of queries) given a fixed model and attack.
In statistical terms, the standard error on the estimation of the mean decreases as $\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}$, where $N$ is the number of samples.
With 1000 randomly selected images, the standard error is sufficiently small to ensure that the reported metrics (e.g., accuracy under attack) are statistically sound. Increasing the test set size would proportionally reduce variance but **would not qualitatively change the conclusions**.
Moreover, in particular for the ASR, since the success can be modeled as a Bernoulli random variable, the variance of the sample mean p (i.e., the ASR) is known in closed form, $\mathrm{var}(\bar{X}) = \frac{p(1-p)}{n}$ (where p is the probability of attack success, i.e., the ASR). Therefore, the worst case is for ASR $\approx 50$\%, where the standard deviation  would be $\sigma_{50}=\sqrt{\frac{0.25}{1000}}\approx 1.58e-2$. This is an upper-bound, which means that the $95\%$-level confidence intervals $I_p$, for an ASR of $p$, would be always included in $[\bar{X}-2\sigma_{50},\bar{X}+2\sigma_{50}]$, i.e., the attack-success rates  $a_1$, $a_2$ of two methods that differ more than 6.32\% can be considered statistically different. 

_Action_: We will include a more detailed analysis of the confidence intervals in the supplementary material.


**Trivial implementation.** We invite the reviewer to check Table 4 in the appendix provided with the original submission. This table provides an overview of the papers that utilized non-homogeneous pools (HeS)  and robust targets (HoS+R), showing that these choices are (unfortunately) not commonly included in evaluation protocols. Our goal in proposing a benchmark is to reduce this gap in future evaluations and avoid propagating this bad practice. 


[1] Stutz, David, Matthias Hein, and Bernt Schiele. "Confidence-calibrated adversarial training: Generalizing to unseen attacks." International conference on machine learning. PMLR, 2020.

summary.value: This paper introduces TransferBench, a comprehensive benchmark designed to evaluate ensemble-based black-box transfer attacks in adversarial machine learning. These attacks generate adversarial examples using a set of surrogate models and may optionally refine them through limited queries to the target model. The authors argue that prior evaluations have been overly optimistic, often using surrogate models architecturally similar to the target and excluding robust models from consideration. To address this, TransferBench offers a structured evaluation across 17 settings on CIFAR10 and ImageNet.

strengths_contributions.value: Based on my understanding of white-box adversarial attacks, I find that the authors have carefully identified and articulated common pitfalls in evaluating the robustness of target models. Moreover, they conducted a systematic and well-structured evaluation across a broad range of black-box attacks, with fair and transparent comparisons.

limitations_weaknesses.value: I would be interested in seeing experimental results across different perturbation budgets $\epsilon$, as this would provide a more comprehensive understanding of the attack robustness under varying threat models. However, I understand that due to the space limitations of the paper, including such results in the main text may not be feasible. In that case, I encourage the authors to provide an extended analysis in the supplementary material or in future iterations of the benchmark.

I would encourage the authors to include the relevant results in the revised version to further strengthen the claims.

summary.value: The paper introduces a framework called TransferBench to assess ensemble-based black-box transfer attacks in scenarios that have been underexplored in previous research. Through extensive experiments conducted within this framework, the study reveals three key findings: attack success is closely linked to surrogate model selection and ensemble diversity, state-of-the-art attack methods perform poorly against robust victim models, and query-based refinements from target models do not lead to significant improvements in attack performance.

strengths_contributions.value:
The paper makes a valuable contribution to the growing body of research on ensemble-based black-box adversarial attacks. It offers a comprehensive empirical investigation into how surrogate model design choices influence attack transferability—a critical but underexplored dimension in adversarial machine learning. Below are the key strengths of the paper:
- The paper addresses an important gap in the literature by focusing on surrogate model characteristics as a key determinant of black-box attack effectiveness and offers a fresh perspective that complements existing approaches.
- The authors effectively position their work within the broader context of adversarial attacks and clearly articulate how their approach differs from and extends previous studies. By identifying limitations in current benchmarks and methodologies—such as over-reliance on specific model architectures or narrow experimental settings—the paper justifies its methodological innovations and underscores the need for a more holistic evaluation framework.
- A major strength lies in the breadth and depth of the experimental setup. The authors define a range of attack scenarios and carefully construct corresponding baselines. This level of detail enhances the credibility and robustness of the findings.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
- The experimental analysis primarily focuses on the marginal effects of individual factors on attack success rate. However, it does not systematically investigate potential interaction effects between these variables. Specifically, the impact of one factor  might be highly dependent on another. Without such an analysis, the conclusions drawn from the experiments may be incomplete or potentially misleading when applied to more complex, real-world scenarios. A more thorough factorial or ablation study that accounts for interactions would strengthen the empirical foundation of the work and provide deeper insights into how different components jointly influence the effectiveness of black-box attacks.

- Tables 2 and 3 show that the query-free method SASD\_WS performs comparably to query-based baselines under certain settings (e.g., HeS scenarios), which is an intriguing result. However, the paper does not sufficiently clarify whether this outcome reflects a generalizable trend in ensemble-based black-box attacks or if it is contingent on specific design choices in the current benchmark setup. For example, the performance parity could be influenced by the choice of surrogate models, the structure of the proposed ensemble framework, or even peculiarities of the datasets used. This raises concerns about the external validity of the finding and its applicability beyond the current experimental context. The authors should consider discussing the limitations of the current evaluation framework and provide theoretical or empirical support for the broader relevance of this observation.

ethical_considerations.value: Yes, there are ethics concerns that require attention by the authors

ethical_comments.value: The paper acknowledged potential misuse but lacks detailed safeguards, and the paper should include more concrete safeguarding strategies for responsible dissemination of the tool, especially given its application in adversarial machine learning.

dataset_code_comments.value: The paper provides openly accessible evaluation code and maintains an online leaderboard. It also includes a detailed README file and a well-structured project architecture with comprehensive unit tests, ‌collectively enhancing‌ the reproducibility of its findings.

additional_feedback.value:
- The paper omits discussion of the HeS+R scenario - could the authors clarify this methodological exclusion?
- The paper could use the factorial analysis method in the DoE to extend the findings from statistical perspective. 
- The paper should explicitly define the meaning of variable z in Equation (3) and clarify its relationship with  g(x) in Equation (1).

final_justification.value: The authors did not include numerical results on the correlation of design factors from my first concern, but the qualitative response adequately addressed my concerns, so I maintain my original evaluation score.

summary.value: This paper introduces TransferBench, a benchmarking framework designed to evaluate ensemble-based black-box transfer attacks in a more realistic manner than previous studies. The authors argue that existing evaluations are biased due to overly optimistic scenarios, such as using surrogate models that closely resemble the target model or not considering robust target defenses. TransferBench addresses these shortcomings by incorporating diverse surrogate-target combinations and robust targets, ultimately revealing that many state-of-the-art methods fail to perform well under these more challenging conditions. The findings highlight the limited effectiveness of query-based refinement strategies in enhancing attack success rates, challenging previous assumptions in the field.

strengths_contributions.value:
* The motivation is clear.
* The paper is well-written and easy to follow.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
Lack of Innovation: The main findings presented in the paper (such as higher transferability in homogeneous scenarios and lower transferability in heterogeneous scenarios) are relatively intuitive and have already been widely discussed in the literature. Moreover, in the evaluation of black-box attacks, heterogeneous scenarios are themselves the most basic evaluation method. The evaluation scenarios proposed in the paper are essentially not innovative. The main contribution of the paper lies in the integration of existing scenarios to achieve one-click deployment and usage, which is more of an engineering improvement rather than a breakthrough or innovation in black-box attack evaluation methods.

Limitations of Attack Scenarios: Although the TransferBench framework covers multiple attack scenarios, in real-world applications, attackers may face more complex and dynamic environments. For example, target models may be continuously updated and enhanced with new defense mechanisms, and the evaluation scenarios designed in the paper may not fully cover these practical situations. Therefore, as mentioned above, the paper lacks substantive innovation in scenario design.

Applicability of the Benchmark: While TransferBench is significant in promoting more accurate and comprehensive attack evaluations, its applicability is somewhat limited. The framework mainly focuses on specific types of attacks and scenarios, and may not be directly applicable to other types or more complex attack situations, requiring further extension and improvement.

Compatibility with New Attack Methods: As adversarial attack techniques continue to evolve, new attack methods are constantly emerging. TransferBench needs to be continuously updated and expanded in terms of its evaluation scope and standards to ensure its effectiveness and adaptability to new attack methods. Otherwise, its value as a benchmark testing tool will gradually diminish.

title.value: TransferBench: Benchmarking Ensemble-based Black-box Transfer Attacks

TLDR.value: We introduce TransferBench, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating ensemble-based black-box adversarial attacks under realistic scenarios, revealing limitations in surrogate model choices, robustness generalization, and query efficiency.

abstract.value:
Ensemble-based black-box transfer attacks optimize adversarial examples on a set of surrogate models, claiming to reach high success rates by querying the (unknown) target model only a few times. In this work, we show that prior evaluations are systematically biased, as such methods are tested only under overly optimistic scenarios, without considering (i) how the choice of surrogate models influences transferability, (ii) how they perform against robust target models, and (iii) whether querying the target to refine the attack is really required.
To address these gaps, we introduce TransferBench, a framework for evaluating ensemble-based black-box transfer attacks under more realistic and challenging scenarios than prior work. Our framework considers 17 distinct settings on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet, including diverse surrogate-target combinations, robust targets, and comparisons to baseline methods that do not use any query-based refinement mechanism. Our findings reveal that existing methods fail to generalize to more challenging scenarios, and that query-based refinement offers little to no benefit, contradicting prior claims. These results highlight that building reliable and query-efficient black-box transfer attacks remains an open challenge. We release our benchmark and evaluation code at: https://github.com/pralab/transfer-bench.
